tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Crop sorghum and escaped shattercane have broad leaves and terminal panicles varying from tightly packed grain heads to open branched heads. Trace the rooted annual crown, then inspect a branchlet for a larger sessile fertile spikelet beside a stalked companion. White midrib, grain color and head compactness are NOT species-proof.
tiles.short: Robust annual Sorghum; verify the actual base and paired spikelets
tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROSS CUE; CONNECTED BASE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK THE ROOTS
tiles.details: Flora of North America describes S. bicolor as annual or short-lived perennial, generally without rhizomes, with culms 50–500+ cm. In established S. halepense colonies, look for persistent jointed creeping underground rhizomes. The existing rhizome comparison panel depicts OTHER SPECIES Johnsongrass, not S. bicolor. Do not infer absence of rhizomes from a cut stem.
tiles.short: Typically no long scaly rhizomes; Johnsongrass has them
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CONNECTED S. BICOLOR ROOTED CROWN

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: At the inner blade–sheath junction find the actual membranous ligule, approximately 1–4 mm in published FNA treatment, and check for absent auricles. The Rasbak S. bicolor collar photograph is archived as panel 2, but it is not millimeter-calibrated; do not arrow an unverified membrane edge or substitute the S. halepense comparison collar.
tiles.short: Membranous ligule about 1–4 mm; no auricles

tiles.heading: 04 · EXAMINE A PAIRED SPIKELET UNIT
tiles.details: Published FNA ranges: compound panicle 5–60 cm, branchlet with 2–7 sessile/pedicelled pairs; fertile sessile spikelet ~3–9 mm, pedicelled often staminate or sterile ~3–6 mm on a 1–2.6 mm stalk. Photograph a connected mature pair at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler. Panel 3 shows actual S. bicolor flowers but does not independently establish all attachment points.
tiles.short: Sessile fertile spikelet 3–9 mm; pedicelled partner 3–6 mm

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT GLUMES AND LEMMA
tiles.details: On one mature sessile spikelet separate the two enclosing glumes from the lower sterile lemma and the thin upper fertile lemma. Published USDA/FNA treatments describe the upper lemma as roughly 1–5 mm, varying from awnless to one bent/twisted awn about 5–30 mm. An awn arises from the lemma, NOT a glume. Awn presence and glume hairiness vary among cultivated and feral forms; the current gallery has no scale-verified dissection.
tiles.short: Two enclosing glumes; upper fertile lemma may be awnless or bear a 5–30 mm awn

tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT JOHNSONGRASS AND SHATTERCANE
tiles.details: Johnsongrass (S. halepense) forms persistent perennial patches from scaly rhizomes. Feral shattercane belongs to the S. bicolor complex and may shed mature grains readily; cultivated grain sorghum often retains them. Neither purple color, pale leaf stripe, loose head nor shattering alone reliably separates all forms. Compare the actual crown and mature paired spikelets before a species-level determination.
tiles.short: Rhizomatous perennial versus nonrhizomatous crop/feral annual; grain shattering varies

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: CROP SORGHUM (S. bicolor): generally ANNUAL, robust erect cane-like culms, broad flat leaf blades and upright crop/forage PANICLES of widely VARIABLE tightness. The individual Sorghum inflorescence units include a fertile sessile spikelet and a pedicelled partner; examine attachments and grain glumes under 10–20×. Distinguish Johnsongrass S. halepense by its deep CREEPING SCALY RHIZOMES and perennial colonies, not by red-purple panicle or pale blade stripe. Shattercane feral forms of S. bicolor may shatter ripe seed and resemble Johnsongrass: a mature seedhead or vegetative view by itself is NOT definitive.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Find the actual branched terminal sorghum panicle attached to a broad-leaved culm: dense crop or loose feral heads are both possible.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At the inner blade–sheath junction find the actual membranous ligule, approximately 1–4 mm in published FNA treatment, and check for absent auricles. The Rasbak S. bicolor collar photograph is archived as panel 2, but it is not millimeter-calibrated; do not arrow an unverified membrane edge or substitute the S. halepense comparison collar.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Published FNA ranges: compound panicle 5–60 cm, branchlet with 2–7 sessile/pedicelled pairs; fertile sessile spikelet ~3–9 mm, pedicelled often staminate or sterile ~3–6 mm on a 1–2.6 mm stalk. Photograph a connected mature pair at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler. Panel 3 shows actual S. bicolor flowers but does not independently establish all attachment points.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Johnsongrass (S. halepense): persistent scaly underground rhizomes in established plants. Shattercane: weedy S. bicolor forms that shed mature grain more readily than most domesticated grain sorghum; panicle compactness varies and cannot reliably distinguish them.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: Moadeeb's licensed Austin/Texas photo shows a horizontal whitish underground stem with segmentation and attached roots.
